newsitem.title: CANADA: NorTel sees '97 sales growth above 14 pct.
newsitem.headline: NorTel sees '97 sales growth above 14 pct.

text.p: Northern Telecom Ltd sales will be above the 12 to 14 percent minimum growth target band the company has given to analysts, president and chief executive Jean Monty said on Monday.

"We will go through it. We will grow by more than 12 to 14 percent, which is the range of minimum growth that we had put out to the analysts. That's top-line," Monty told Reuters in a post-earnings telephone interview.
"And the bottom line will grow by more than the top line. Margins will improve," he added.
Monty said he felt good about 1997.
Monty said he was pleased with the company's performance in 1996.

"If you look at the order growth...41 percent in Q4 in orders, that's quite significant. When you look at the backlog, US$6 billion going into the new year. I think these are all record numbers," Monty said.
"Revenues have grown at 20 percent (in 1996) -- we're a sizeable company to be able to have a growth rate at that level. And earnings continue to grow faster than revenues," he said.

NorTel's sales rose 20 percent to US$4.19 billion in the fourth quarter of 1996 from US$3.50 billion in the year earlier period. Net earnings per share rose to US$1.23 from US$0.98 in the fourth quarter of 1995.
Order input for the fourth quarter was a record US$5.27 billion, a 41 percent increase from the US$3.74 billion in the year earlier fourth quarter.
For the year, the company posted sales of US$12.85 billion, 20 percent higher than the US$10.67 billion in 1995. Net earnings rose to US$2.40 a share from US$1.85 a share in 1995.
Monty dismissed an initial tumble in NorTel's share price. The stock was recovering in late morning after analysts came off the company's conference call.
"You know, I think the stock market will analyze this thing and I think in the end they will like it," he said.
On the Toronto Stock Exchange, the stock was at 92.40, off 1.20, after falling to 90 in earlier action. In New York, NorTel fell 3/4 to 68-5/8, up from the session low of 66-7/8.
Monty said the high concentration of sales and earnings in the fourth quarter -- something analysts raised red flags about in the past -- was improving.
In 1996, 51 percent of earnings and one-third of sales occurred in the last quarter of the year.
"It used to be a lot more than that. As time goes on, there's no question that the mix of customers that we have permits us to think that we can (normalize that) gradually," Monty said.
